utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue to hear the evidence, the Chamber was informed that the Prosecution had two preliminary matters to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just a few simple matters relating to Witness Kralj who, you'll remember, back on the 28th of October testified as a liaison officer with the Main Staff. And one of the convoy documents used, P06864, did not have a complete translation. We've now completed the translation. And it is in e-court at doc ID 0676-9828-A-ET, and we'd ask that that be uploaded. We've informed the Defence and everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Uploading is what you're supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's uploaded and we would just like it in. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to attach doc ID 0676-9828-A-ET to P06864. The translation was the only issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's one other thing. And that, of course, replaces the -- the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it about the same document what are you raising now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. Then let's finalise this one first. P6864 with the new attached translation is admitted into evidence. And, Mr. Lukic, as always, you've got 48 hours to revisit the matter if the translation causes you any concerns. Next one, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, you may remember when the Defence put in a document, D728, which was a convoy -- which was actually a combat report from the Rogatica Brigade which indicated a UNHCR convoy, they had found a few boxes of ammunition on it, and you had asked us to look in to see if there was a complaint filed with UNHCR about this particular situation. And you said that it might assist the Chamber in its assessment and evaluation of this piece of evidence. So we went back and looked, we didn't find any UNHCR documents. We did find a few UNPROFOR documents that talked about this convoy, and that we did identify a few issues that might help you look into the matter further. I've found four documents that I've shared with Mr. Lukic that provide some information. I could briefly tell you what that information is to see if you want to look into it any further. It's rather simple information, though. It's the kind of thing that sometimes creates more questions than answers, but it does answer part of your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you discussed what you would bring to our attention, Mr. McCloskey, so that it is, I would say, neutral in terms of what is in those documents? I mean, apart from what that means and what conclusions you could draw from that. Is there any disagreement about the content?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, there is no disagreement about the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement about relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. There is none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Then, Mr. Lukic, I suggest that Mr. McCloskey brings to our attention a few facts which apparently are not in dispute and is about issues found in documentation. And if there's anything you'd like to add, then, of course, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. McCloskey, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just 30 seconds to tell you what this is, really, and see how far we want to go with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. Yes ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggested, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We did find that this convoy referred to in this document we believe was -- left from Belgrade on June 7th and that it was escorted by a Russian contingent and that it was designed to go to Zepa, and that -- we understand from the document that UNHCR is investigating the finding of the few boxes of ammunition, but we didn't have any results of any investigations. I thought it was interesting to -- for you to know that it originated from Belgrade and it was -- it got stopped outside of Zepa where the boxes were found and it was escorted by a Russian contingent of UNPROFOR, which I think creates questions about how that ammunition got there and what purpose it was. But that's what we found out about it. I basically have that information in four documents which I could offer into evidence if that would be helpful or not. I find this matter relevant but I don't find it overly important regarding the issues, though any question you have is obviously important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, first of all, I do understand that there's no dispute that these documents at least indicate that the convoy left from Belgrade, that it was accompanied by a Russian contingent of UNPROFOR, and that was designed to go to Zepa where it was then stopped before arrival. That information doesn't allow you at this moment for conclusions, Mr. McCloskey, but rather raises issues as how, when, where, and by whom got that ammunition on the convoy. Do we need the documents for that, Mr. Lukic? I'm looking at you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. McCloskey just tried to comply with your request if we can find anything, so I think it's more for Your Honours to decide whether Your Honours need those documents or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, to the degree that we may see other convoys that have ammunition found in them, this might be an issue that we would bring up, but I'm comfortable not offering these documents unless you'd like to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, this party -- this -- these facts found in those documents on which the parties at least agree that the documents tell us that these were the facts, the Chamber does not need the documents themselves at this point in time. If at any -- if in the future it would be useful or would be helpful to have a closer look at those documents, either in view of other evidence that emerges or whatever, then there's still a possibility that -- that you tender them and that you -- or you file them or you tender them at that point in time. At this moment, we do not need the documents. We are satisfied with the information on which the parties apparently agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's on the record. And it's also clear on the record that what I said is an agreement between the parties. Then, Mr. McCloskey, anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One small matter. I see Mr. Stojanovic is no longer with us. Oh, no, there he is. Thank you. We had -- there's an old intercept matter. There's -- that I believe we have agreement on. P1366 is an intercept that we had offered a revised translation for. Basically it came down to the translation said: "This job gets an A." The original translation was always: "This job gets an A." In one of the revisions it got turned into: "This job gets a 5," and that's what's currently in the record. I believe Mr. Stojanovic has agreed with me that the appropriate translation should be: "This job gets an A," and if we have that agreement, then we will make sure that translation is uploaded and put in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently there's agreement. We're waiting for the new translation to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're not sure. I thought there was but we had a little trouble communicating, so I -- we need to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there agreement on the portion of the translation where Mr. McCloskey says it should be: "This job gets an A," where there may be at this moment doubt as whether the "job gets a five."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the agreement we reached yesterday, Your Honour. And it was my understanding that we had agreed to meet up today as well in this regard, and to define how this would be possible. Actually, how possible to stipulate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the easier thing is if it's a translation issue, that the new translation will be uploaded, that we get a number for that, that Madam Registrar is then instructed once we know that number to attach it, and that it would then replace the current translation and then we have a new P1366 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I had provided Mr. Stojanovic with the -- with the old and the new, and we'll discuss that to make sure we get that and do as you say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand this morning it's easier to agree with the Prosecution than to agree within the Defence. Mr. Lukic, nothing from the Defence any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have nothing to raise today, Your Honours, and I think that my colleague will meet with Mr. McCloskey in the afternoon to discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for the results of that. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And that would be Mr. Todic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent there may be any uncertainty, the document, the translation which is now attached to P06864, is replacing the old translation. So it's not only that the new one is attached but the old one is removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Todic. Mr. Todic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for the Prosecution [sic]. No saluting, Mr. Mladic, you know that. No saluting. Just refrain from doing it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I think you said that I'm for the Prosecution here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I said so, then it's -- I don't know whether it's a comedy of errors or a tragedy of errors, but, Mr. Lukic, apologies. I'm a fully aware that you're here for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Todic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your name and surname, slowly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: I'm Dusan Todic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D1686 in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todic, did you give a statement to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that. I gave the statement on the 16th of May, 2013, and the 19th of January [as interpreted], 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that page, do you see the signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: My very own personal signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at the last page of this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature or signatures on this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes, in both places you can see my signature. And the date is the 19th of June, 2014. That's when I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todic, does this statement correctly reflect what you said to General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is contained in the statement, is it correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I've given an oath. I said that I would speak the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you, in principle, provide the same answers as you gave when this statement was written up?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN TODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'd offer this statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1686 receives number D798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just read short statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todic witnessed the attack of the illegal Slovenian Territorial Defence on the JNA unit and facilities, managing to pull out with his unit to Pula during a cease-fire and then by ship to Bar, Montenegro, from where he reached Batajnica, Serbia. He will testify that from Batajnica he went via Bihac to Knin, where he witnessed the attack of the illegal Croat forces on the JNA units and Serbian civilian population in Dalmatia and Knin Krajina. Due to a lack of men, General Ratko Mladic often asked security organs to accompany him in the front. That is how he personally witnessed and took part in the events concerning the pacifying of the separation line from Cetina village via Sibenik to Zadar, Posedarje, Maslenicki most, and Mali Alan. Using a megaphone, the General called both sides to agree on cease-fire, not to shoot but to negotiate. Mr. Todic stayed in Croatia from 27 August 1991 to 12 May 1992, when he went to Crna Rijeka together with General Mladic and Colonels Tolimir and Zivanovic. He worked with the intelligence and at the Security Administration. He was engaged as personal escort to General Manojlo Milovanovic. He visited all the war theatres with him. Mr. Todic will testify about the rape of Serb women in Gorazde, which he personally heard at the positions around Gorazde, and about medical assistance provided to an ill Muslim girl from Gorazde, her treatment at the Military Medical Academy and the military hospital at Pale. He will also speak about the captured unit of Muslim boys of the 5th Corps of Army of B and H, which General Mladic returned to Bihac in 1994 without exchange. He will testify that General Mladic never ordered any attack on civilian objects in his presence, not even when they watched together as the Muslims burned the house of Mladic's parents. He will testify that General Mladic always insisted on a fair and proper conduct towards prisoners of war. Mr. Todic will also confirm that during the activities at Srebrenica, he was with General Milovanovic at the western Krajina theatre of war. They both came to VRS Main Staff between 17th and 19th of July, where he was present during short conversation between General Mladic and General Milovanovic. That was the statement summary of this witness, Your Honours, and I do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're aware that you added a few things to the statement, such as the qualification that attacks were illegal, et cetera. That's not in the statement itself. But as again the statement is not the evidence, we'll focus on what we find in the statement. Thank you for that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the fact that Mr. Lukic doesn't put any questions to you doesn't mean that your evidence is not important for us, but we find it all in your statement, and Mr. McCloskey will now cross-examine you. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Witness, I do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- of course, now the question arises why this witness was not called as a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, because he was testifying about General Mladic, so it's, I think, our understanding that he cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's acts and conduct of the accused. I fully agree with you, Mr. Lukic. You're perfectly right. You could not even have called him under Rule 92 bis, but that's due to the content and not to the fact that you have no further questions for him. Nevertheless, let's not forget that Rule 92 bis does not apply if the statement is about acts and conduct of the accused because Rule 92 bis creates a possibility to call the witness without being cross-examined. But if there's no need to cross-examine him, then, of course, one could consider - and that has been done in other cases as well - it could have been put before the Chamber whether it would be a solution under those circumstances where there's no need for cross-examination to admit into evidence the statement of the witness without any further questions being put to him and without the witness being cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you, only this is the first time that this situation arose so we couldn't anticipate it in any way. But we will approach the Prosecution with several witness statements for we consider that could be 92 bis although it has some testimony about General Mladic. But we'll discuss it with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least it is a matter to be considered because the ultimate result now is that the witness travels to The Hague in order to find out that his statement is summarised in court, that no questions are put to him, and that he travels back to the former Yugoslavia, which is certainly not the most efficient and the most -- and the most -- we were not here to save money but we're also not here to spend money on matters which do not in any way further the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I just may add before my colleague responds, Your Honour, it was estimated two and a half hours for cross for this witness, then it was cut down to half an hour, and only now we learn that there is no questions for him, so we could not avoid bringing him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're perfectly right in drawing my attention to be perhaps a bit more critical to the Prosecution with having indicated two and a half hours, then half an hour, and now nothing. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this -- I notified the 30 minutes several days ago, so I think everyone was on notice of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the issue is whether there was any need to cross-examine the witness because if there was any need to cross-examine the witness, the Defence was under an obligation to call the witness to be present to be cross-examined. If you still had doubt on your mind whether or not you would have any questions, then you should have raised that in a timely manner so that the Defence could have acted upon such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as I'm sure you're aware, this is a very important and strategic decision the Prosecution makes and it was not made until just a few minutes ago when I saw that this person had nothing extra to add to you. And I'm certainly not going to take the time in this court when I don't need to. But this is an important decision. I do not take it lightly and -- but it's a strategic decision. There's a lot riding on this decision and whether or not re-direct is going to happen, whether or not they are going to lead witnesses in the future, this is an important decision. It is not something we did lightly and I just made it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could the parties, in the future, in relation to witnesses where there's any chance at all that there will be no further questions in-chief, that it's only the statement which is tendered, nothing in addition to that, and where the Prosecution is strategically considering whether it would cross-examine the witness, yes or no, to at least discuss the matter so as to avoid that the witness spends a lot of time on coming to The Hague and that the Tribunal spends a lot of money on getting the witness to The Hague and then to find out in court that nothing is added to the statement itself. We leave it to that. Witness, I -- Mr. Todic, you've heard the discussion I had with the parties. I had this discussion because I feel it not the best way to proceed in asking a witness to come a long way to The Hague and then to find out that, apart from the statement he has given already, that no further questions are there and that, therefore, the whole travelling exercise, both cumbersome for you and expensive for the Tribunal, is -- was unnecessary. I just want you to know that. I also want you to know that we highly appreciate that you took the effort coming to The Hague, and that you were willing to assist this Chamber in determining the issues in this case by giving your evidence. I can't say more about it. Thank you very much. And you may follow the usher, and I wish you a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that it be checked. I asked yesterday that the witness be ready for transfer at 10.00. Now I see it's eight past 10.00. I'm not sure he has been transferred to the building of the Tribunal. I would now appreciate it if somebody could check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness is expected to arrive in two minutes from now. I suggest that we take a very short break, that everyone remain standby so that we can resume, if need be, within the next three, four, or five minutes. We take a very, very short break. --- Break taken at 10.08 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijanovic. Before you give evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mijanovic. Mr. Mijanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the standard procedure here in court, would you please give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, did you at one time give the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic a written statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask to call up in e-court 65 ter 1D04150. Could we look at the last page of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, I hope you see it before you now. Is the signature on this page and the date written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, in the course of proofing before you appeared in the courtroom today, did you indicate that three corrections should be made to your statement, to make things more precise?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at the first paragraph in the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, please have a look at it. We read here that you are currently employed in the Republic Directorate for Renewal and Development and you told me that the exact name of the company where you work, the Republic Directorate for Renewal and Civil Engineering. So one word, "development," needs to be changed into "civil engineering." Or building. Thank you. In paragraph 2 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness answered yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, in the last-but-one line, you mention a name whose last name -- a man whose last name is Sonja, S-o-n-j-a, whereas you said that the correct name was Sunje, S-u-n-j-e. Would that be the correct name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4 of your statement, in the last-but-one sentence, we read: "After coming to Ilidza, for a while I provided security for the municipal building ..." You have said, though, that a more precise phrasing would be: "Upon coming to Ilidza" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to object now actually. We have not received a proofing note so -- as far as I'm aware, so I'm not aware of these corrections. But on this -- I see the first two were kind of technical matters, but on this sentence I'd actually ask that if the witness has a correction, that he just be asked what the correction is in an open-ended fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I do understand you will follow the suggestion made by Mr. Weber. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I thought this was a minor correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But I will ask you, Witness, to tell us what kind of work you did after coming to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: After I came to Ilidza, I did not provide security at the municipal building as written in this text. Instead, I occasionally served rounds of duty at the TO Staff which was in Sumarska Aleja, in that local building, and that building would later become the staff of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would then a more precise phrasing be instead of: "For a while, I provided security to the building" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, leading, I believe it will be as it started out. Also it's asked and answered. He's been asked to provide his correction and he's provided his correction for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Weber is insisting on you not leading the witness in this respect and you should abide by that. I mean, abide by the rule, not to abide by what Mr. Weber says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. If what the witness said is sufficient for the time being, I will ask no more about this correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now, Mr. Mijanovic, having made these three corrections, would you still today, after making a solemn declaration in the courtroom, give the same answers to these questions and would your answers be completely accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender the statement of Witness Slavko Mijanovic, which has the 65 ter number 1D04150.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on the matter. Witness, you were shown the last page of your statement, and you were asked whether the signature on the page and the date written is in your hand, and you confirmed that. Do you have any recollection of signing the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was here, in January 2013. I don't know exactly which room. Maybe during proofing or preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you -- you say it was here in The Hague, and you said it was January. Was the 19th of January, 2013?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19 January, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could I take you to your statement. I do see that you start with the paragraph with your own background, et cetera, and then it goes on. Paragraph 11 still deals with the time after August 1994 until the Dayton Agreement. Is that all correct? You had an opportunity to re-read it? And perhaps we could have the third page of the statement on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You checked everything very carefully, that there are no mistakes in this statement? Apart from the corrections you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there's a whole item which is: "Information received since 19th of January, 2013." I have some difficulties in understanding how you can sign a statement on the 19th of January of 2013 in which you relate what information received after the 19th of January, 2013. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. In the B/C/S version, it is clearly stated there is no word "after." It says: "Information obtained on 19 January 2013."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that is the case, then -- well, I checked in the B/C/S whether at least the date was there. Now it seems that you confirmed that the date is there. Could we have the -- it reads: "Informacije" -- let me try to do the following. I'll read the B/C/S or the witness could read the B/C/S. Could you read what is said there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Information received 19 January 2013." Should I read on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no need to do that. This resolves the matter. Mr. Weber, you were sufficiently familiar with the language to already understand that this was what was meant. And that you asked for a correction of the English translation, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No. But I appreciate that this was the Karadzic statement so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- there's no dispute about that. Mr. Stojanovic, we then need to have a new translation uploaded, which says that it is information received on the 19th of January, 2013. Then I have one question: From whom did you receive that information, on the 19th of January, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I received this information from anyone. I knew about all of that, and I supplemented the information that had been written up here earlier on. I wrote this entire information at some point after Dayton - I don't know exactly when - having no idea that it would reach this Tribunal. Then, during the preparations, I supplemented the information with this. That is to say, I was familiar with this from the very outset. It's not that I received it from anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Had you been interviewed before the 19th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 19th of January, someone asked me to write up this information that I did. In addition to being asked to come to testify before the Tribunal and the preparations that I had here, no one else ever discussed the matter with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that the whole of the text is your own formulation. It is not that you were interviewed and that this text was written down by someone who interviewed you, but you were invited to put on paper yourself what you knew and you added the last three paragraphs on the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wrote this information which is essentially the same as this one, except that I did not deal with it in a lawyerly manner because I'm not a lawyer. I'm an architect. And then one of the lawyers here, one of the Defence counsel, let me put it this way again, dealt with it in a lawyerly fashion, wrote up these paragraphs, et cetera. But my information and the one that we have before us is the same, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to the statement of the witness would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement bearing number 1D4150 receives number D799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification, awaiting a new translation to be uploaded. And the Chamber notes well that there is no objection to admission. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic -- yes, we are at the time for a break. Witness, further questions will be put to you after the break. We'll take break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking at a volume audible for others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read out the statement or, rather, the summary of the statement of Slavko Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Slavko Mijanovic has a university degree in architecture and, as an SDS official, in the autumn of 1990, he was appointed deputy secretary of the Secretariat for Town Planning and Housing Affairs in the municipality of Novi Grad in Sarajevo. He remained in that position until the end of April 1992, when, for safety and security reasons, he left his job, moved his family to Montenegro, and he went to Ilidza and made himself available to the War Commission of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza. The witness says that because of intensive war operations, Ilidza was being abandoned both by the Serb and non-Serb population as they were fleeing from the horrors of war, seeking a safer environment. Some of the non-Serbs stayed on in Ilidza throughout the war and, at the same time, a lot of the Serb population started coming from the territory of the Muslim part of Sarajevo; that is to say, Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija as well as Central Bosnia. So it became necessary to provide accommodation for these people and to have abandoned apartments placed under municipal control. With that objective in mind, the War Commission of the municipality of Ilidza, in July 1992, adopted a set of rules on providing such apartments for temporary use. These apartments were supposed to be distributed by a commission that was headed by Witness Mijanovic. Apartments were allocated on the basis of criteria that defined priorities and these decisions contained a particular clause; namely, that the apartments were being allocated for temporary use until the end of the war operations without the possibility of acquiring ownership rights over these apartments and also that the temporary tenants are duty-bound to take good care of the apartment and the objects found in the apartment. In its work, until the summer of 1993, this commission reached over 3.000 decisions and later on it grew into the Secretariat for Housing Affairs, and the witness was appointed secretary of this newly established secretariat and remained in that position until August 1994. The witness notes that no one's ownership or tenancy rights were ever infringed upon. And after the war, everyone had their tenancy rights returned. So, in accordance with the law, it became possible to buy these apartments and to transfer these ownership rights. That would be the summary of this statement, and, Your Honours, with your leave, I would just like to put a few questions to Witness Mijanovic. Could we please have a document in e-court. It's been marked for identification as D899 [as interpreted]. I would like us to focus on paragraph 5 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding, Your Honour, was D799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you say already after the second big attack by Muslim units on the Serb part of Ilidza municipality on the 14th of May, 1992, and then you continue about that. I would just like you to tell the Court, to the best of your recollection, when this first attack of the Muslim units occurred against the part of the territory was controlled by the Serb forces in the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first part was on the 22nd of April, and I know that from the documentation that was included in the mentioned rules on the allocation of apartments. Although I, on the 22nd of April, was not in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 -- so please let us take a look at paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can keep this part of paragraph 9 in English because I'd like to focus precisely on that first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that: "The Secretariat for housing and municipal affairs made a list of the flats, determined their condition, and compiled a database," et cetera. Could you tell us whose apartments these were that you registered?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The database as far as these apartments are concerned in the urban part of Ilidza had already existed in the Secretariat for Town Planning and Housing Affairs, or whatever its name was. The secretariat had a complete register and compiled records on the ground. That is to say, every effort was made to collect correct information about the structure of the apartments, the tenants of the apartments, the owners of the apartments because it was mainly companies that were the owners of apartments, whereas it was physical persons who had tenancy rights. No attention was paid to ethnic background and that was not recorded in the database at all. In the briefest possible terms, all the apartments were registered in the urban part of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What are the apartments that you had available when you allocated these apartments for temporary use?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The apartments that are categorised as abandoned apartments, regardless of who owned the apartment and who had the tenancy rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 15 - let us please take a look at paragraph 15 of the statement - you say: "After the war, everyone's tenancy rights were recognised, so people were allowed to buy and sell these flats in accordance with the law." Could you please tell the Trial Chamber if you have more precise information; namely, the return of property in the municipality of Ilidza to the pre-war owners or tenants, was that fully carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to say a few words about the decisions that I signed, the decisions on the allocation of apartments for temporary use. These decisions are accessible to you, and it is visible that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- witness, the question was about what happened with the apartments, and the question was related to paragraph 15, where you say: "After the war, everyone's tenancy rights were recognised and people were allowed to buy and sell these flats in accordance with the law." Now that is what the question is about. Would you please first answer the question, whether that was fully carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the post-Dayton or, rather, post-war period, speaking of Republika Srpska, according to statistics, all tenancy rights were restored as well as ownership rights over all immovable property. If there were individual cases otherwise, it's a play of numbers that can be explained by a statistical margin of error. What I do know is that there was no reciprocity on the side of the Federation because military-owned apartments were never returned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, you were not asked to comment on what happened on the other side. You were asked, I think, about Ilidza, although you expanded your answer on other areas as well. Let me put the question quite simple: What was the number of apartments with ownership rights of Serbs - and later I'll put the same question for you for Muslims - that resulted in moving out of the owner and finally not either moving in by the owner again or the apartment being sold by the owner? And let's start with Serbs. If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilidza municipality is idiosyncratic in the sense that under the Dayton Accords, the central urban part of the municipality where I was in the war went to the federal side, went to the Federation, whereas the eastern part, Kasindol and Gojkovici went to the Serbian side. So it's hard to talk about an exact number. And what I said about the level of Republika Srpska, I know these things because I had a close co-operation after the Dayton Accords with the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. Do I understand that you do not have precise, detailed information about whether the rights that were to be observed fully, whether that -- whether that took effect, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have such information in its entirety but this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have it for any part of Ilidza, because it was split up? Would you know it for one part or for the other part of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less both parts of Ilidza. That's where ownership rights and property were fully returned or restored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means that everyone returned to his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That does not mean that everyone returned to their house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does it then mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that people managed to get their property back but physically they did not return. Because they cannot earn a living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have detailed information about how they got their property back even if they did not return to it? Did they sell it, or did they ... was it let to others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to sell their property beforehand, in accordance with the law and legal regulations, one had to have one's property returned, and many people sold their property, exchanged it, and carried out other legal action. Ilidza nowadays belongs to the federal part and it is a fact that very few Serbs live there nowadays. Most of them are elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are many Muslims now living in the part of Ilidza which belongs to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the part of Ilidza that belongs to Republika Srpska, it so happened that there weren't many Muslims. They were the minority population there. What I see is that, to a large extent, these settlements are now populated. And after Dayton, I became the chief of town planning in that area, and I personally legalized many buildings and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. These settlements are now populated by whom? Still by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still by the Muslims, where they lived. Not to the extent to which they lived there before, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. To what extent? What percentage did return to their own property? Do you have any statistics about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The return was 100 per cent. But which percentage truly lives in their pre-war homes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do you know the return was 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because I worked in the municipality as chief of town planning, and in that directorate I have constant contacts and co-operation with the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons and the Ministry for the Human Rights of Refugees at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what percentage now lives -- truly lives in their pre-war homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not say exactly. But I'm coming back again to that story that I issued many decisions after the war concerning the legalization of unlawfully razed buildings, about the paving of roads because it was a rural area, and for the building of new housing. And I'm talking about the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to my question. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court how that part of the pre-war Ilidza municipality is called, the one that went to Republika Srpska and is mainly inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The name is Kotorac. I cannot really distinguish between upper and lower Kotorac. And also in Kasindol there was some Muslim population, and Ilidza also came to include a good part of Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV. These were neighbourhoods that used to belong to the pre-war municipality of Novi Grad. Since these are large buildings with a large number of tenants, the ratio of inhabitants was 50-50.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point, you mentioned military-owned apartments or army-owned apartments. What do you understand by that term?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Housing owned by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and were given or allocated to military personnel for their use, but even before the war, under some law, some of these apartments were repurchased and became the private property of those who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijanovic. At this moment we have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, today I'd like to start by discussing your involvement in the functioning of the Ilidza municipal government and just your role within that government. Is it correct that you attended meetings where members of the municipal Crisis Staff were present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Crisis Staff and I did not attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff, but I was on the premises --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't exactly my question. I just want to know: Did you attend meetings with individuals who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend the official meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please carefully listen to the question. The question, as clarified in the second round, was whether you attended meetings with individuals who were members of the Crisis Staff. That is, did you attend meetings where other persons were present who were members of the Crisis Staff, not necessarily Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you attended meetings where other persons were present who were members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nedjelko Prstojevic is a member of the Ilidza -- was a member of the Ilidza Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: President of the Crisis Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend meetings where Mr. Prstojevic was present during the entire war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the statement that you just gave is not accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was accurate. Nedjelko Prstojevic was the president of the Crisis Staff and later president of the municipality. I, as a member of the Executive Board or a member of the commission or later secretary, attended many meetings together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You scheduled meetings of the War Commission in Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when they were held at the time when I was on duty service. On the instructions of Mr. Prstojevic and according to the list given me, I called members to attend meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. Just to clarify your last answer, the person who called these meetings was Nedjelko Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the original phrasing of paragraph 4 of your statement, which I understand you've made some clarifications to, you stated: "After I came to Ilidza, for a while, I provided security for the municipal building in Ilidzanska Aleja where the Crisis Staff and the military command had their offices." So I understand the clarification that you made about your responsibility. I'd like to ask you about the other part of this sentence. The municipal building that you're referring to is in the same building as the SDS hall; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if it assists the witness, I see the statement is before him, D799, I'm referring to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building in the Ilidza Aleja is not the municipal building. The municipal building is about a kilometre away from this one. In that month of May, when I came to Ilidza, there was nobody in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you for a whole explanation. My question -- you're referring to this structure as the municipal building. Is this the same building where the SDS hall was located? That's what -- those were located in the same place, correct? The building you are referring to and the SDS hall.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the SDS or the SDS hall, and it was nothing to do with the SDS. The Crisis Staff was in the forestry house, in the forestry lodge, in Sumarska Aleja. There is no such thing as an SDS building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That seems to be inconsistent, your last statement with your -- with the statement in your written statement. You described the municipal building in your statement, and you said it was where the Crisis Staff and the military command had their offices. This is correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. In my correction to the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the correction to the statement we made at the beginning of this session, I stated that I did tours of duty at the telephone in a building in Ilidzanska Aleja which housed the Crisis Staff and which was later to become the headquarters of the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. I'll go with your last answer now. The military command which you say later was there, that was the command of the Ilidza Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 15675 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up on the screen is a summary of the minutes from the third operational and consultative meeting of the Ilidza Serb municipality from 28 July 1992. We see that you were present at this meeting with a number of other individuals, including Mr. Prstojevic. We see that item 2 on the agenda, which a little bit lower on the page, related to the organisation and operation of municipal administration organs. Is it correct that you and Mr. Prstojevic worked together on issues related to the operation and organisation of municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you knew Nedjelko Prstojevic from before the war when you were the under-secretary for urban housing matters in Novi Grad and Mr. Prstojevic was the secretary for housing inspections in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The second name on this list is Radoslav Unkovic. Mr. Unkovic was also a member of the Ilidza Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of both versions. Your Honours, for -- so you're aware, I'm going to be referring to the bottom of the page in English which is the top of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, on this page, we see a section entitled: "The task of the work group." The minutes refer to the tasks of this group including one being to have contact with the government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the issues of creation of policy and ways of utilizing financial assets. Is it correct that there was co-ordination between the policies created at the local municipal level in Ilidza with those of the government of the Serb republic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be positive. There was some co-ordination, although from what I know, throughout the war, we in Ilidza felt a bit neglected and the co-ordination with the authorities in Pale was not the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll discuss this a little further in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 15675 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 15675 receives number P6941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You mentioned this on direct examination and it's in your statement, specifically paragraph 6, where you indicate that in July 1992 the War Commission of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza adopted the rules of procedure on assigning flats for temporary use. As the president of this commission, were you -- did you participate in the drafting of these regulations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm president of the commission, not the War Commission. These things were normally done by legal experts from the municipality. I can't remember exactly, but I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31630 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is -- are the regulations on the allocation of flats for temporary use to the families of killed or wounded combatants, refugee families of combatants and other people adopted by the War Commission of Ilidza Serb Municipality on 5 July 1992. These are the rules that you referred to in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to go through a number of articles of this document with you. The first one I'd like to discuss with you is Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the lower part of the B/C/S original. Article 3 states: "In accordance with the decision on the return of displaced persons to the territory of the Serb Republic of BiH ... the following people are considered displaced: People who did not return to their place of residence by 20 May 1992" - if we could have the next page, thank you - "nor justified the reason for not returning. This resulted in the loss of all their employment, their rights for medical and pension insurance, and the tenancy rights." I'll just read the last sentence: "Also, they do not have the right for citizenship of the Serb Republic of BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this definition of displaced persons mentioned here includes non-Serbs who left Ilidza prior to 20 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This - what is it? - decree, or what, was never enforced, not in a single case. This never actually came into force and nothing was ever done under this regulation. Nobody ever had their rights to employment or citizenship rescinded. The government never enforced this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you, you are using two terms. You said that actually never came into force. And you say it wasn't enforced, which is not the same. Was it adopted and was it -- was it an existing legal tool, irrespective of whether it was ever enforced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the regulation -- at least this part of the regulation was based on -- on that decree. Whether de jure it ever entered force, I don't know. I know, though, that we never worked following this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ignored existing legal provisions? Is that what you're telling us? You were not abiding by what may have been the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot say that after this decree or whatever it's called, I mean, very probably a different one was soon adopted that annulled this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours, since a decree is mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness. Yes, we would have to ask the witness what he referred to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I would just like us to see for that purpose the first and the last page of this document. I think it would be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In English it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this is a matter of fairness to the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 3 in the beginning, if we may see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see the last part of Article 3 on your screen at this moment, I think. If you'd-like to have the beginning. Could we move to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of Article 3. So it's not a decree. It's a decision on the return of displaced people to the territory of the Serb Republic of BH, Official Gazette of the Serbian people of BH, et cetera, et cetera. When I was talking about a decree I was, in fact, referring to this decision. I just didn't know what it was called exactly. This decision was never enforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Probably. Because it's written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you -- I don't think you've really answered my original question, which is that this provision, as written, would have applied to non-Serbs that had left Ilidza prior to 20 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what is written here. What is referred to here is the return of persons who had moved out. Their return to the territory of the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure I see the same language that you see here. I see that: "The following people are considered displaced: People who did not return to their place of residence by 20 May 1992" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read this out to you: "Decision on the return of displaced persons on the territory of the Serb Republic of BiH ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, you're invited not to interrupt Mr. Weber. Second, what Mr. Weber is drawing your attention to, he will read that. Carefully listen to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to this article, it refers to the following people are considered displaced: "People who did not return to their place of residence by 20 May 1992, nor justified the reason for not returning." I'm just going to stop there. Unquote. This would have applied to non-Serbs who left prior to 20 May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. That pertained to the entire population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which includes non-Serbs that had left, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Serb and non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I suggested to you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to go through Articles 6 and 7 with you. Article 6 starts on the bottom of the page before you. Pursuant to Article 6 of the regulation, it identifies three categories of people for whom flats may be allocated. All three of these categories refer to families of combatants. Before I move on to the next page, have you had the opportunity to review these categories? Have you read all three categories?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have the next page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 7, people who gained the status of combatant are identified as those who joined the Army of the Serb people of BiH or the police force of the Ilidza Serb Municipality. Is it correct that the references to combatants in these regulations relate to members of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Ilidza MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both the MUP and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "both the MUP and the army," is it correct you are referring to the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska, and when you say MUP, you're referring to the Serb police forces, the Serb MUP in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Flats were not allocated to families or members of the ABiH or HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since we're on this page, I'm also going to briefly discuss with you Article 9 of the regulation. It states: "Those families are not -- are considered to be refugee who left the territories of Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica, Novi Grad and other war-stricken areas and who have registered on the territory of the municipality and whose able-bodied family members joined the Army of the Serb people of BiH on the territory of Ilidza Serb Municipality." Is it correct that this refers to the Serbs who came to Ilidza from the other areas mentioned in this section? I believe you've already discussed Serbs leaving these areas during your examination.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31630 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31630 receives number P6942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just for timing, I'm going to go through some quick documents before the break and skip something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll come back to something with you a little bit later, but I just want to go through a couple of other documents quickly. Flats were provided to Serb volunteers who were present in Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you said "flats were provided."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what "Serb volunteer" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's been corrected. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware of Serb volunteers present in the Ilidza municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about people who arrived from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm talking about people who were volunteers, were considered Serb volunteers, who were mobilised as part of the Territorial Defence in Ilidza municipality in April 1992 and who formed part of the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska after that. Those are the people I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: For me, in accordance with these regulations, these are either soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska or members of the MUP of Republika Srpska, or persons who have work obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is there any confusion, that the witness thinks that we're still talking about the previous document and that you put a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- question to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is unrelated. So understand the question without thinking back to the document we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I'll just go to a very specific example. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 11359 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is a 9 July 1992 War Commission approval from Nedjelko Prstojevic. According to the approval, the use of the motel facility in Gladno Polje and the deserted summer houses in this vicinity are approved for the needs of the Serbian volunteer units. The second paragraph specifically refers to the commander, Branislav Gavrilovic and indicates he will be conducting admission and training of Serbian volunteers arriving to this area. This is just four days after the regulations we just saw. Is it correct that the War Commission approved accommodations and facilities to Serb volunteers, including Mr. Gavrilovic? These are the people I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 11359 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 11359 receives number P6943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6943 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, before you go to your next document, if you can deal with it in two minutes, which is unlikely, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I think you're right as usual on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take another break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you'd want to deal with another document which already can be shown on the screen, I would ask for it now already. It is just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Prosecution -- the next document -- I did have a question before we got to this document, but the next document I'll be referring to is 31632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you know Tomo Kovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31632 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to -- since you've mentioned these decisions, I just want to look at an example of one of them. Before you is a decision by the president of the commission for the distribution of apartments dated 31 August 1992. Do you recognise the signature appearing at the bottom of the page to be yours?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Ask this an example of the decisions that you would issue during the war to allocate housing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the heading there's reference to pursuant to Article 13 of the rules on assigning apartments for temporary use. Those are the 5 July 1992 regulations that we looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under the statement of reasons, you say: "Given the fact that he has been participating in the defence of the Serbian republic since the beginning of the war and that, currently, his family has no accommodation, the commission for the distribution of apartments has decided as stated in the disposition of this decision." Did you personally determine that Tomo Kovac deserved the allocation of the apartment of the three-bedroom apartment for this reason or was this a decision that was made by someone besides yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was made by the commission. I signed it as president of the commission. And Tomo Kovac had to bring documentation so that there would be confirmation of the status of a refugee or displaced person and also of being engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska or, rather, in the defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So whenever someone was allocated an apartment, your commission verified that they had something to do with the war efforts on behalf of the either the Army of Republika Srpska or the Ilidza MUP. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to engagement in the Army of Republika Srpska and in the MUP, also there could be certificates of work obligation, and in this way, people could have apartments allocated to them for temporary use.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So, for example, when you refer to work obligation, if someone worked at the Famos factory in special-purpose production or something of that nature, that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not only war factories but any factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31632 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 31632 receives number P6944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, in paragraph 6 of your statement, you state: "In the period between April and June 1992, when the migration of the whole population of Ilidza municipality was at its most intense, but also throughout the rest of the war, the authorities of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza and their organs did not expel non-Serbs. They moved out of their own accord and in an unorganised manner." Is it correct that the most intense period in which non-Serbs moved out of Ilidza was between April and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4581. I will be going to page 66 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
