utterances.text: Sir, before you are Nedjelko Prstojevic's statements at the 17th Assembly Session of the Republika Srpska held between the 24th and 26th of July, 1992. Focusing on Mr. Prstojevic's comments which in both versions are on the bottom half of the page, he states: "I have decided to say a few words and to ask a few questions that I am being asked by the citizens of Sarajevo. Namely, when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government or at least it was not known where it was then." After Mr. Prstojevic discusses President Karadzic and his visit to Ilidza, Mr. Prstojevic goes on to state: "The Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory, and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a [sic] majority." Sir, is it correct that Mr. Prstojevic's statements back in July 1992 contradict your evidence that the Muslims moved out on their own accord? You agree with that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He spoke generally about the town of Sarajevo. It is possible that there were municipalities where people were expelled. He never says Ilidza. They were not expelled from Ilidza. And Ilidza did not expand its territory either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, the Ilidza Crisis Staff implemented policies related to the movement of Croats and Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P470 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that this does not deal specifically with Ilidza, could you tell us what were the territories where the Muslims were driven out in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a hard question for me. I know that they were not expelled from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes. And you do not know whether Mr. Prstojevic -- to what territories referred? Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he was in Ilidza, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as why he would have referred to other parts of Sarajevo where he was -- had his responsibilities in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously there was some animosity between the government and Mr. Prstojevic or, rather, Ilidza. He says that he doesn't know where this government is and so on. Obviously that this is some kind of objection that no one knows where this government is and that Serbs were self-organised in various municipalities. He's talking about Sarajevo here, not Ilidza. He as president of the Crisis Staff had more information than I did. I mean, objectively speaking. I was a completely new man in Ilidza in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could he have known more about Ilidza than you did know and that, therefore, he included Ilidza in his statement about territories in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read here that he included Ilidza and I never heard of that. At any rate, he had comprehensive information about Ilidza, where he lived and worked before the war, where he was president of the Crisis Staff, and throughout the war, he was president of the municipality. So he had all the information available as I could not have. I arrived in Ilidza and I only knew the urban central part of Ilidza, in part, and I didn't even know where the peripheral rural areas were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so the Prosecution's position is clear to you, it is our position that Mr. Prstojevic as the president is referring and including the municipality of Ilidza. Do I understand -- do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but that is not something that I came to realise on the basis of the text that was read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at more documents then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have -- P470 is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to this. This is a 19 May 1992 decision from Nedjelko Prstojevic of the Ilidza Crisis Staff. In the first paragraph about the decision there's reference to a meeting held on 18 May 1992. Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what meeting this might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us know if it comes back to you. The decision begins: "The moving out of Croats and Muslims from all territories of Ilidza Serb Municipality is allowed ..." Were you present at a meeting on 18th May when this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I wasn't. But it is a fact that in May everybody could move out of Ilidza. Even into town, to Serbia, Montenegro. I don't think that there were any restrictions. Both Serbs and non-Serbs were moving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This decision only refers to Croats and Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The decision continues: "Apart from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica (prohibited from leaving)." Is it correct Croats and Muslims from these areas were not allowed to come to Ilidza according to this decision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica were not under the control of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza. I do not know how this could possibly apply to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question. Croats and Muslims from these areas, the three areas that you've now mentioned again, were not allowed to come to Ilidza according to this decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Serbian Ilidza had no authority over these areas. What we read here is there is no exit. It's under the control of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, where do -- can I find a reference to coming to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm focusing your attention is on the decision. It states: "The moving out of Croats and Muslims from all territories of Ilidza Serb municipality is allowed." And then it goes on to say: "Apart from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica (prohibited from leaving)." What I'm putting to you, sir, is that this decision indicates that Croats and Muslims from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica were being prohibited from leaving those areas and coming to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last portion is -- where do we find that in the -- in the decision, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- the whole decision. Apart from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm putting my case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are also putting the text of a decision to the witness in which you fill in elements which are not literally found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not intending to do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If I'm not clear in my questioning, then I'm happy to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm on my feet, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Mr. Stojanovic's witness but I don't want to interfere. I just want to clarify there is one translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no prohibition in B/C/S version so maybe it should be read first and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we ask the witness then to slowly read the first sentence after the word "decision," after "odluku."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The moving out of Croats and Muslims from all territories of Ilidza Serbian Municipality is allowed, except for Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica (no going out)." This phrasing is incorrect. Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica were never part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, you were not asked. You were only asked to read the lines. Now, Mr. -- I do understand that the word "prohibited" is not there but there is a similar language, that is, no moving out. Whether that is a fact or whether that it normative, I wouldn't know at this moment. Wait for the next question to be put to by Mr. Weber and answer that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that is what the decision states, then that would probably clarify my question. So I'll move on. I'll have -- I'll ask that we have this checked, the language. It's P470.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Serbs that wanted to move to Ilidza from these areas - Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica - were allowed to come to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Already in the early days, in May, there was a separation line between these neighbourhoods and Serbian Ilidza. The question arises how anyone could have passed through these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is an interesting question, perhaps, but not an answer to the question that Mr. Weber put to you. Those Serbs who wanted to move to Ilidza from these areas, were they allowed to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say anything for certain, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put that actually that's an incorrect statement, and even pursuant to the regulations that we looked at, it envisaged Serbs coming from these areas, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, and Hrasnica, and being mobilised in either the military or police. Do you have any other comment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. This is completely incorrect. Just as non-Serbs could not move out towards Hrasnica, Butmir, and Sokolovic Kolonija, the Serbs could not go the other way. It's another conversation entirely, how people managed this or that. But the separation line lay through there and that's exactly where the 14 May attack happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, a minute ago you told us, "I can't say anything for certain." And now, a few lines down, you say it is "completely incorrect," which puzzles us, because on the one hand side you say, "I don't know for certain;" on other hand, you say it is "completely incorrect."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, in paragraph 6 of your statement you say: "Due to strong and intensive war operations, Serbian and non-Serbian residents left Ilidza to escape from the horrors of war in search for a safer environment." And then you go on to state: "And at the same time, Serbian refugees were coming in from the Muslim part of town of Sarajevo, Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija," and then you go on to say Central Bosnia and so on? So, sir, I'm perplexed here. Serbs were coming from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija into Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But there is a date up to which it was possible to get out but after that date, not. After 14 May, after the attack, it was not possible to get out. These people had left the town earlier. I'm talking about mass evacuations from Hrasnica, Butmir, and Sokolovic Kolonija. As far as I'm concerned, the real war began on 14 May, and even on that day people were going to work and coming back to their homes, moving towards the centre of the town. Not all but some.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we have your various answers now, and I'm going to go and continue looking at some more things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 20803 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is an intercepted conversation from 23 May 1992 between Nedjelko Prstojevic and Milosav Gagovic. This conversation takes place four days after the decision we just looked at. The part I'd like to discuss with you is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions. Toward the bottom of the page in both languages, and this is after Mr. Prstojevic refers to his neighbours in Sokolovici sunbathing in their cellars, Mr. Prstojevic states: "However, these people should know about Ilidza policy." Gagovic responds: "Yes." Prstojevic then states: "We have a sort of big, the highest municipality." Gagovic says: "Certainly." Prstojevic states: "We have our policy in the area of Sarajevo." Gagovic says: "Certainly." Prstojevic states: "Our policy in relation to refugees from Sarajevo." Could we please have the next page. Gagovic responds: "Fine." Prstojevic states: "All the Serbs, men, women, children, adults, will be accepted by Ilidza." Gagovic responds: "Fine." Prstojevic then states: "And shall be accommodated." Gagovic then responds: "Okay." Prstojevic states: "Accommodation, food and the rest." Gagovic responds: "Fine." Prstojevic states: "Secondly, no Muslims shall be allowed to leave Sarajevo." Gagovic responds: "Sorry?" Prstojevic states: "We shall not allow the Muslims to leave Sarajevo." Gagovic then responds: "Fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you're familiar with the policy that Mr. Prstojevic is discussing during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I am talking only about Ilidza. I'm thinking of Ilidza. It's not logical for Serbs from Sarajevo to move to Ilidza. I don't know where he got that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I put it to you that this conversation is consistent with the decision that we just looked at and it was, in fact, the policy of the Ilidza municipality to accept Serbs, whether they be men, women, children, or adults, and that no Muslims would be allowed to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about Sarajevo. Muslims had no reason to come to Serb-controlled Ilidza. The fact was that Ilidza was prepared to accept anybody and everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After the non-Serbs moved out of Ilidza in -- in -- between April and June 1992, those were the apartments that you allocated; right? The apartments that were formally occupied by them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The number of people who moved out from Ilidza, Serbs and non-Serbs, were in an approximately equal ratio. And we got the apartments, the abandoned apartments of both ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic [sic], what apparently Mr. Weber is putting to you is that even if in equal numbers they moved out, that Serbs were allowed to move in but Serbs only and not Muslims. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Yes, when I said "Mr. Prstojevic," of course, that was a slip of the tongue. You are not Mr. Prstojevic. That's what Mr. Weber puts to you, that whoever may have moved out, that only Serbs were allowed to move in again and not Muslims. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a comment. Mainly Serbs came in, but there were also individual cases when Croats moved in specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in this telephone conversation, it doesn't say everyone who left is welcome to come back, but it says Serbs can move in. Others should not leave Sarajevo. And if you can't leave Sarajevo, then you may find difficulties in going back to Ilidza. Apart from whether it may have happened once or twice or a limited number of cases with a Croat, this is the overall picture which is pointed to you on the basis of this telephone conversation by Mr. Weber. Any further comments than the one you gave already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. But it's completely illogical for a non-Serb to come to Ilidza and then not be able to get in, because Ilidza was encircled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 20803 into evidence. And so the Chamber has a complete record, as part of the Karadzic proceedings, this intercept was authenticated Mr. Prstojevic himself and that can be found in the Exhibit P2521 in the Karadzic case. So I'm just providing that further information so the Chamber is aware of it. And we do have a CD of the intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard of no objection by the Defence. Therefore, Madam Registrar, could you assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 20803 receives number P6945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's -- yes. The audio is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- provided to Madam Registrar as well. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P2770 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be another intercepted conversation. This one is between Rade Ristic and Nedjelko Prstojevic. The date of the conversation is 25 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the bottom of page one in the English - and if we could please have the top of page 2 in the B/C/S - Mr. Prstojevic states: "All that is Muslim to be killed, like Alija." He then goes on to say -- and if we could have the next page in English: "I don't" -- and actually the -- the English says: "I don't one to see one military-aged Muslim alive there." And then he goes on to say: "Secondly, immediately, I give you ... authorisation to give Muslim apartments to Serbs there." And then he refers to part of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you see these statements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that, in fact, Mr. Prstojevic was providing authorisation to give Muslim apartments to Serbs in Ilidza, and that's what's reflected in these statements. You agree; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this -- these comments here, Mr. Prstojevic says: "I give you the authorisation to give Muslim apartments to Serbs there." This is what -- what was happening; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I clarify this a bit? Rade Ristic, with whom Prstojevic is talking, is a man from the rural parts, from Vojkovici village which was physically completely cut off from the central part of Ilidza where the municipality was. To go to Vojkovici you had to use a macadam road for 70, 80 kilometres. Vojkovici did not have any socially owned housing. Those were free-standing houses. It's an area that used to belong before the war to Novi Grad municipality. There was fighting there, and I visited perhaps two or three times during the whole war. Those were buildings where the separation line cut through the building. One floor was held by the Muslim forces, and another floor by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you've given a long explanation. You haven't answered my question, but based on what you just said, I'll draw your attention to what Mr. Prstojevic says next. He says: "Every Serb that is fighting there can, on your recommendation, even if this housing situation is not sorted out, we already have the forms printed out, if you will fill it out, he'll immediately get an apartment assigned to his name." Ristic responds: "Aha, all right." And then Mr. Prstojevic states: "And you should know, over here in Nedzarici is already happening, we are filling out 30 forms today." Sir, Nedzarici is not by Vojkovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nedzarici also used to be part of Novi Grad municipality before the war. But the Kasindol Street connects it physically to the centre of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, this Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about this geography so I'm not going to labour it with you, but I'm going to ask my original question to you based on Mr. Prstojevic's comments. Based on the fact that 30 forms a day were being filled out or we were filling out 30 forms on this given day, is it correct that authorisation was being given to Serbs to give them the Muslim apartments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ristic obviously procured this authorisation, although I don't think it was really implemented because it was on the separation line. Who would be prepared to move into such apartments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you really haven't answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have additional follow-up, I was going to move on. I've asked my question a number of times. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 03802 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a decision by Nedjelko Prstojevic for the War Commission of Ilidza Serb Municipality and we see at the bottom it's dated 4 April 1993. The decision begins: "At its third regular session held on 3 April 1993, considering the problem of the return of Croats and Muslims, the War Commission of Ilidza Serb Municipality passed the following ..." Before we discuss the contents of the document, did you attend the session of the War Commission on 3 April 1993? I'm sorry, 2 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't possibly be. I was not in Ilidza on that date at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The body of the decision states: "The return of Muslims and Croats to the territory of Ilidza Serb municipality is forbidden for security reasons, as well as because the necessary conditions for their return do not exist." During the war, I put it you that the Ilidza War Commission did, in fact, forbid the return of Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written here, although I can't understand why people would be returning to that chaos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whether -- the issue is not whether they wished to return but whether they were forbidden to return, and you apparently do not disagree that that is what this decision says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I give an opportunity to the witness to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you would agree that this document clearly states that the return is forbidden for Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 03802 receives number P6946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 22766A for the witness. And we're actually going to go to the transcripts of this exhibit. The first page is fine in both versions. Your Honours, I'm going to try to complete this one exhibit and then that will be the conclusion of my examination in the next ten minute, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is transcript of a SRT news broadcast of a meeting in the Ilidza municipality, when President Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Velibor Ostojic visited the municipality for presentation of the Famos 2FB engine in the opening of the Information and Technical Centre of the SRT in the western part of Srpska Sarajevo. According to this transcript, Nedjelko Prstojevic made the opening remarks and he was followed by speeches by Mr. Miroslav Berjan, the managing director of Famos, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Krajisnik, and then lastly, President Karadzic. To possibly help you with some context for this news broadcast, Mr. Prstojevic was also shown the video corresponding to this transcript prior to his Karadzic testimony and he indicated that this event occurred on 8 January 1995. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 4 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today I'm just going to discuss with you some of President Karadzic's statements at this event. His speech begins at the bottom of the page before you. President Karadzic begins: "We are determined," and then there's an unintelligible word, "strategic aims which our assembly adopted to get separated and we have separated and formed our state. But some changes have to happen in very Sarajevo in a way that Serbian areas go to Serbs in its entirety by means of political negotiations and talks, in a way that the -- that Serbian city will be formed and separated as a whole, in a way that the former Sarajevo is transformed into two cities." Sir, one of the Serbian areas that President Karadzic is referring to here as having to go to the Serbs is the Ilidza municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: If that is what is written, then that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you aware of the Bosnian Serb strategic aim to separate Serb and non-Serb populations throughout Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the Bosnian Serb strategic goal of dividing Sarajevo into two cities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After discussing what Mr. Karadzic or President Karadzic views as a peaceful resolution to the situation, he goes on to state: "If our neighbours do not show enough understanding, we will decide for ourselves how big Srpska Sarajevo and what will be in Srpsko Sarajevo, and then we," unintelligible word, "Sarajevo is a city and a city in Republika Srpska because all the land Sarajevo is situated on is Serbian and all the surroundings are Serbian. And if they do not want to come to a quick solution, the whole Sarajevo will be Serbian in the end. We think that a more favourable variant for us is if they do not agree, and a more favourable variant for them is to agree because in the long run, their part of the city, which has no outer border, has no any prospects." These statements by President Karadzic indicate that the Bosnian Serbs had no intention of returning the outer parts of Sarajevo already considered Serbian; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In fact, these statements show that President Karadzic hoped the Bosnian Muslims did not agree to give the areas surrounding Sarajevo to the Serbs because this would allow the Bosnian Serbs to claim the whole of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't make me confirm things that I don't think myself. What's the date of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of our knowledge, this is from the 8th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that's after Dayton, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's not -- that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I've read it to you and it's before Dayton. If you're not aware of this, I'll accept your answer on that. Is that -- is that how I should understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 22766A into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 22766A receives number P6947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, with that, the Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Stojanovic, could you give us an impression as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall reorganise during the break that follows, Your Honour, but I think that it's going to be about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Which means there may be some time left to start hearing the witness of the next witness, if that witness is -- has arrived. If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is not here and is not scheduled for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to work with him in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So he would be available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Witness, re-examination will be conducted after our break. You may follow the usher and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you are ready, you may start your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document P6943 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mijanovic, the Prosecutor asked you about this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would just like you to tell the Court what kind of building is this, when there's this reference to motel in Gladno Polje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is a building that was owned by some orchard. It was an orchard that was state-owned, socially owned, whatever it was called. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This building, state-owned as you say, would that be a residential building and would it be included in the rules on the temporary use of apartments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. It does not invoke the rules. It does not invoke the rules on allocated apartments for temporary use. And it seems to me that the commission hadn't been established then, or maybe it had, but most probably it hadn't. And it doesn't invoke the rules. Although, in my practice, I did have a case when a member of - what was its name? - Brne's unit would come and ask for an apartment for temporary use. This unit, they were, you know, like a bad pupil about to be expelled from school. They were expelled from this orchard, and this person would have to have a certificate stating that he was a member of the MUP or the army or that he had the status of a displaced person. And as far as I can see, the rules are not being invoked here at all, and as far as can I see, the document was signed by Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go on, Witness, you do say this might have been -- the War Commission might have been established or not established at the time. The heading here says: Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ilidza Serbian Municipality War Commission, and the signatory signs there as the War Commission. Which commission are you saying was not established yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commission that I headed, that worked on the basis of the rules. That is to say, this decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this same document, the War Commission, inter alia, is referring to this unit that is within the MUP and is allowing them to use abandoned weekend cottages that are close to the motel. Can you tell us whether you know at all who the owner was of these abandoned weekend cottages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at document P6944. P6944.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, if you remember, it's that decision of the commission. It has to do with the allocation of an apartment to Tomo Kovac for temporary use. Can one see from the statement of reasons whether there was any deviation there from the obligations stemming from the rules on allocating apartments for temporary use?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also have to meet the same requirements? Was it compulsory for him to receive this only for temporary use and appropriate use?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a standard form. It's just the name and surname and the square metres of the apartment, et cetera, that are changed. But it's a form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm going ask you now: According to the rules on the allocation of apartments for temporary use, was it possible to allocate an apartment to someone who was not a soldier or veteran?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber under which conditions an apartment could be allocated for temporary use to someone who did not belong to this category of soldier or veteran?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was sufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I missed it, if counsel could refer me to the part of the regulations where that is discussed just so I can know for further questioning if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, did you have anything specific on your mind or did you have the absence of any provision for that on your mind? And if you have a specific part on your mind, would you please inform Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, nothing specific. Just clarification of the way in which this commission worked and in the context of the question as to who could receive apartments for temporary use. This is what the Prosecutor asked during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rules were the only document on the basis of which these decisions were being made. By the very nature of things, it wasn't that comprehensive. It could not include the entire subject matter that would crop up in the field. In addition to soldiers and veterans, according to the rules, people who had work obligation in different companies could also be allocated apartments. Further on, residents of the immediate war zone could receive such apartments too because it was unsafe to use their apartments or houses or if their apartments had been devastated during war operations. Also in the rural parts of the municipality of Ilidza, people came from Zenica, Kakanj and other places in Central Bosnia, and they were allocated abandoned houses, barns and so on, because over there they lived in similar conditions too. All of this could not be defined in the mentioned rules. It was only a year later that the government passed a decree with the force of law. Something like lex specialis for this kind of work. Our rules, however, were passed a year before that and somehow they fitted into the framework of that decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work in this commission for the allocation of apartments for temporary use, did you ever have any instructions or requests for allocation to be carried out on the basis of some kind of discrimination against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's been a very long time. I cannot remember exactly, but I think these rules included something like the discretion of the president of the Crisis Staff that he could allocate a certain number of apartments. I'm not sure, but I think there's something like that. One could not do this kind of work without being fair to a maximum. Otherwise you couldn't survive. It was such a difficult thing to do. To this day, I think that my seat was the hottest one in the hell of war during those days. There were a few cases, I think, when I didn't want to sign a decision, but Mr. Prstojevic would sign these documents. However, it wasn't on behalf of, et cetera. The signature actually did say: Nedjelko Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As president of that commission, were you ever told that you may not allocate an apartment to a non-Serb if he was from a family of a fallen fighter or a veteran or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I also allocated apartments to such persons. It concerns small numbers again. The Latin saying says: "Nomina sunt odiosa," names are not desirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are not going to insist, but if it becomes necessary, we will ask you for names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you said "small numbers," what do you have on your mind? 1, 5, 50, 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one case involving a Croat, a Croat family throughout the generations, not a case of a mixed marriage, and there were at least 15 – 20 cases of mixed marriages, but the owners of tenancy rights who got apartments for temporary use were Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if I read your statement well, some 3.000 decisions were taken. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's probably my report to the assembly sometime in 1993. That was a report for that period. There was -- there were more decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. More than 3.000, but you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- three cases where non-Serbs were provided with housing: Two mixed marriages, one Croat family, no mixed marriage. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: One pure Croat, so to speak, and there were several people from mixed marriages. I didn't say two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- at least the transcript reads "at least two cases," which means that there may have been more, but at least there are two. Is that correctly reflecting what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't. I don't know exactly how many such decisions there were, but there were more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking just whether what is in the transcript reflects what you said. Because if you say it does not, then we have the opportunity to check that on the basis of our audio registration and then we would know whether you said something else, whether you said not "at least two" but whether you said something else. Do you want us to verify that? Or do you admit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say "at least two." I said more. Or several.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, with your leave, I did hear what the witness said, and I believe it's fair to listen to the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have that verified, whether the transcript is accurate or not. We'll verify that, Witness, because it would be unfair to you if we find something on the transcript which is not what you said. Could you then give us -- if you say it was more than two, could you say, was it four, five, three, ten, 50, any further indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the ones that do you remember, do you have the names of those families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andjelko Raguz, pre-war police officer, had a house on the Federation side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry to pop up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- but could we just have confirmation that the spellings are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- first. Could you please spell the name, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andjelko, A-n-d-j-e-l-k-o. Last name, R-a-g-u-z, Raguz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said he had a house on the Federation side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did your commission also deal with houses on the Federation side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm slightly confused how you would say this was one of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. He left his house, he left the federal territory, came to the Serbian entity as a refugee, continued to work as a policeman until the end of the war and living in the Serbian territory on -- and on that basis, he received an apartment for temporary use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still -- let me see whether I understand you. Yes, he continued to work as a policeman for the MUP in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he was -- although being a Croat, he was -- he was employed by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know of any examples of persons who were provided with accommodation not being of mixed marriages, not being employed by the Serb authorities but just because they had lost their home and then non- -- not being Serbs? Do you have any examples of such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not easy to distinguish who is Croat, who is Serb. Unless we had personal knowledge about this, we didn't look for it, so I can't say for certain. Serb and Croat names are often identical, and even last names are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no idea whether there were any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I will finish with one more document: P6946.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, this document says, and you've had occasion to see it before during cross-examination, it says in paragraph I: "It is prohibited for Muslims and Croats to return to the territory of Ilidza Serb Municipality for security reasons, as well as because the necessary conditions for their return do not yet exist." The question is: Is the reason that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please allow me to put the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you are going to whisper into the ears of the witness what possibly may have been the reason, then that would be leading, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That was one of the Prosecution's concerns, Your Honour. And the other was that "the return do not exist" is what it says. I believe Mr. Stojanovic added the word "yet."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So would you be precise in your language, Mr. Stojanovic, that's one. And, second --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The -- I added the word "yet" because the actual translation should probably be: "The reasons have not obtained -- the conditions have not obtained." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. The Chamber highly appreciates and also is aware of it not being easy to give all the details of the language used in an interpretation which has to be made within split seconds. Mr. Stojanovic, a non-leading question would more likely start with "could you tell us what the reasons are," rather than "is the reason" because that may raise some concerns. Could you please phrase the question in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, kindly tell the Court if you can explain what is understood here by "security reasons"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality, engulfed in war such as Ilidza was, with a mixed population, was realistically not extremely secure for everybody and both one and another community were under threat, and it was for security reasons that I left the city and came to Ilidza myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, in that year, 1993, in April, as can you see in front of you, was it possible for Serbs who had fled from Central Bosnia, Mostar, Konjic, Herzegovina, to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't cross their minds. They would have never fled if they had any intention of coming back. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijanovic, for your answers on behalf of the Defence team of General Mladic. We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Let me just try to understand. You say, more or less, Serbs would never go back to Central Bosnia. You wouldn't -- that was not something they would do. And is that to be understood as that you would not expect Muslims and Croats to go to a Serb-controlled or Serb municipality near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends on the municipality. You have examples of municipalities where the population returned en masse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's talk about Ilidza then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Dayton Accords, Ilidza was haplessly divided so that this part where I was, the central part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's talk about Ilidza, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether -- you explained how illogical it would be for Serbs to return to places which were not Serb controlled, and do you have a similar reasoning for Muslims not returning to Serb-controlled areas in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, nobody returned to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me read to you exactly what I'm referring to. You were asked about Serbs who had fled from Central Bosnia, whether they would return to their homes in 1993. Your answer was: "It didn't cross their minds. They would have never fled if they had any intention of coming back. Of course not." Now I would put the same question for you as to non-Serbs, would it be -- would it come to their mind to return to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then was the reason to forbid them to return, if you say that it didn't even cross their minds to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in practice, they were not able to return anyway. I don't see why they were prohibited from returning. The state was in a state of war. How could they return? They would have to go through a million separation lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, it was decided that they were forbidden to return. Could you think of any reason for such a prohibition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the date: 4 April 1993. 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've done so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This looks to me like 4 April 1992. For 1992, I can think of a reason. For 1993, no. I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether the third regular session of the War Commission was held in 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose it was in 1992, because it was the third session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document is now in evidence. If the parties would have any further data which would shed light on possible mistakes as far as the date is concerned, of course, the Chamber would like to know because that might be important for our interpretation of the evidence given by the witness and the document itself. I've no further questions. Mr. Weber, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to check in the original. The date there appears at least to be clear, 1993, and also the number is 272-93, not 92. But if there's any further information which would shed additional light on that matter, the Chamber would be happy to receive that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the year 1993 appears twice in the document. One in the first paragraph and one at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This then concludes your evidence, Mr. Mijanovic. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the Bench, put to you by the parties, primarily by the parties, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 26th of November, 9.30 in the morning, this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of November, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.13 p.m.,
